title: Gateless Barrier, Case 15: Tung-shan's Sixty Blows
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing uncertainty and impermanence in Zen practice, rather than seeking clear answers or enlightenment as a separate entity. It suggests that powerful experiences in meditation are often conditioned by personal factors and may not necessarily lead to understanding or clarity. Instead, Nomon Tim Burnett encourages listeners to approach challenges with humility and self-awareness, recognizing their own inner critic as a potential teacher and learning to sit with the present moment without resistance.

sentences.text: You know, the same way our monastic day rolls on.
There were duties to attend to and practices to do, and as a new monk you really had to pay attention and try to figure out what was going on around you.
Maybe those of you who are a little newer to this form have a little bit of that feeling: oh, what do we do next here?
What do I do with this spoon?
That was not much instruction, although traditionally it would have been no instruction.
So Dongshan and the new students go along and finish the day.
Work, practice, eating, everything was formalized in the monastery, including bathing, a particular way you do it, and lying down to sleep.
Probably you would be sleeping in the monk's hall, so if we were doing this right we would not leave this room, particularly these three days, except to go out and do our work.
We'd each have a little bed sticking out behind your cushion and a little teeny cupboard to put your things in.
So if you filled your car full of stuff, it wouldn't have fit in the [unclear: "sand"].
Nothing wrong with having a lot of stuff.
Different systems.

So that probably kept Dongshan pretty occupied, just trying to muddle through the day, even though the different monasteries all shared a similar monastic code, but there were different styles in different places.
Sometimes, probably somewhat sadistically on purpose.
One time I was practicing at a Zen center in Zurich, a strong style of Zen.
There's a whole string of centers in Europe that all emanated from one Japanese teacher named Deshimaru, and Deshimaru was a badass apparently, so all his students have this spirit.
I sat down and noticed that the zafus had these little white tags, and it was facing me as I sat down on the cushion.
I thought, well, that's unesthetic, a little tag sticking out, so I spun it around and sat down and did zazen.
There was a little dharma talk in German during the practice.
I recognized a word or two.
Turned out he was talking about Zen mind, beginner's mind, so Geist was in there.
Then we're out in the lobby and the head student comes up to me and starts talking to me in German.
I said, "I'm sorry, I speak German."
Then he switches to English and says, "You should always put the tag on the other side here."
Cool.
Sorry.
Right, so I'm sure Dongshan was encountering more than one of those moments, and those can be upsetting.
On the one hand, it's just information.
Okay, sorry.
I think it was set up the right way and I egotistically turned it around, thinking I knew better.
Stranger here.
We do that all the time, don't we?
I know better.
Maybe not too consciously, but.
And then Dongshan finally made it to bedtime.
The first book I ever read about Zen, which I recommend, is a classic.
It's called *The Empty Mirror*.
It's a Dutch author, a novelist, actually.
Jan van der Weerling, or something like that.
This guy is in the 50s.
He takes the boat to Japan, having heard something about Zen, and somehow stumbles into this monastery.
It's about to have Rohatsu sesshin, and they let him stay for some reason.
He struggles through the first day, endless zazen, and finally gets to lie down.
This is great.
I'm sorry to spoil this for you, but it's so great.
You should read it.
Read the book.
So he finally lies down, oh god.
The lights are turned out, he closes his eyes, bone tired, like he'd never sat zazen much before, probably at home.
And this was hours and hours and hours and hours and hours.
Then he hears all this rustling around him.
It was a monk's hall; they're all lying there in the zendo.
And all the monks are jumping out of bed.
He's like, holy shit.
They're jumping out of bed and going out into the graveyard to practice night sitting.
He'd just gotten through their normal day, and now they were doing the extra stuff because it was Rohatsu, something like that.
And then they sat for a couple more hours in the graveyard.
Yeah, finally got to go to bed.
So I don't know if that happened to Dongshan, but somehow it gets to the end of the day.
And then Wu Men, who collected these stories, comments about what happens next, which isn't in the koan.
He writes:
*All night in the ocean of yes and no, Dongshan struggled to the ultimate.
As soon as dawn broke, he went again to Yunmen, who explained everything in detail.*
So he spent a tough night.
*All night in the ocean of yes and no, Dongshan struggled to the ultimate.* Which is odd English, but Chinese is hard to translate.
And then perhaps he had early morning dokusan, as a few of us did.
Or maybe he was somehow allowed to visit the teacher in his room, which would seem strange.
But that's a common story in these stories, that students are given special access to the teacher because of their incredible potential.
That's part of Dogen's story too, when he went to China in his 20s because he wasn't satisfied with the Zen in Japan.

He connected with the teacher who became his root teacher, Ru Jing, and he wrote in his journal, *Ru Jing invited me to visit his abbot's room anytime, day or night.* Scholars are a little dubious about that.
Why would a teacher in one of these large state-sponsored monasteries, which were quite rule-bound actually, let a foreign monk not have to follow the rules and visit at weird times?
But it's an important part of the story for us.
In our lineage family, we really appreciate accessibility.
We would like our teachers to be down to earth and welcoming, and seeing the great potential in everybody.
While there's some useful power in the archetype of the great Zen master, and all these levels and color coding that we wear and stuff like that, hopefully we hold that lightly and use it wisely.
Although it is powerful, and it is important.
I was talking to somebody the other day who said, "Oh, my gosh, so many priests in [unclear: "this machine"]."
On the other hand, it's just people with different clothing on.
It's interesting, isn't it?
So hopefully we hold it lightly.
I always figure being a little frumpy probably helps.
I've had a few teachers who were very impressive, briefly.
But these archetypes are powerful, and something in us bounces off them and is informed by them and illuminated by them, mirrored by them.
So it's not nothing, all these forms that we follow.
Even if we're setting up a temporary zendo in a basement with a piece of carpet, we want to have it just so, just so.
So maybe Dongshan got to have early morning dokusan, or maybe somehow he had access to the teacher.
And the story goes on.
After this tough night, he's exhausted and shaken.
He really wants to understand what's going on here.
What have I not understood in my practice?
So here's the rest of the koan again.
*The next day, Dongshan came to Yunmen and said, "Yesterday you said you spared me sixty blows.
I don't know where my mistake is."
And Yunmen shouts, "You rice bag, what makes you wander about now west of the river, now south of the lake?"
At this Dongshan got enlightenment.*
The translation I copied in here actually says the word "got": got something.
So this is really impressive.
I think of the monk actually: courageous, humble and honest, right?
You told me something powerful yesterday and I don't get it.
I could feel that it was powerful.
I've been working on it.
I've been thinking about it, lost in my ocean of yes and no, thinking all night.
Please tell me, please, please teach me.
Pretty vulnerable.
So even these stories that have a fair amount of Zen badassery, there's a lot of vulnerability.
And what does he get back?
A Zen shout and an insult and a question.

So this question, "What makes you wander about now west of the river, now south of the lake?", turns out to refer to particular areas of China where there were a lot of important temples and teachers.

I didn't look up the names of these places, but one area is west of a river and another one is south of the lake. [unclear: "Yogan"] Senzaki translates this part not as literally but more helpfully, as Yunmen hollering instead: "You good for nothing.
You just wander around from one monastery to another."
So that's what it's supposed to mean.
You good for nothing, you just wander around from one monastery to another.
So [unclear: "I'm out this doing Sean is enlightened"].
This calls for a word or two, I think, about enlightenment.
We can't avoid that here, which I'm a little hesitant to bring up because it's so fraught with confusion for us.
Is there this thing called enlightenment?
That seems to imply another question: is there something fundamentally wrong with us right now, because we are unenlightened?
And if we do the right practice stuff for long enough and intelligently enough, enough effort will fix it, and we will become enlightened.
Are these stories saying that?
Well, Dogen has a lot to say about this.
Tomorrow morning we'll chant his great text Genjokoan, which has these lines in it:
*The boundary of realization is not distinct, for the realization comes forth simultaneously with the full experience of Buddha Dharma.
Do not suppose that what you attain becomes your knowledge and is grasped by your intellect.
Although actualized immediately, [unclear: "one is"] inconceivable may not be apparent.
Its emergence is beyond your knowledge.*
Comment from Dogen on enlightenment:
*The boundary of realization is not distinct, for the realization comes forth simultaneously with the full experience of Buddha Dharma.
Do not suppose that what you attain becomes your knowledge and is grasped by your intellect.
Although actualized immediately, what is inconceivable may not be apparent.
Its emergence is beyond your knowledge.*
So he's saying a lot there.
Maybe one of the things he's saying is that perhaps it's a little simplistic, a little dualistic, to have this idea of enlightened and unenlightened as totally separate, distinct things.
He opens that passage saying that the boundary of realization is not distinct, not a distinct boundary between unenlightened and enlightened.
I was thinking about this a little bit logically.

If there was a distinct boundary, and enlightened and unenlightened were two separate ways of being, and we are currently unenlightened, having all these ideas about enlightened, wouldn't our ideas about enlightened be inherently wrong?
Because we're on the wrong side of the barrier.
We can't see over there.
We can't even think or imagine over there, if it's that distinct.
But it also doesn't seem right to say that there's no enlightenment.
Enlightenment is all over all these stories, and Dogen is clearly talking about realization and enlightenment all the time, too.
There's no question that sometimes people have significant and powerful experiences in the course of practice.
No question of that.

Those stories are often quite dramatic, so they get selected for and presented and written down and talked about maybe a little bit more than the stories of seven days of nothing happening, or nothing apparent happening.
Because the other thing Dogen says, second sentence: do not suppose that what you attain becomes your knowledge and is grasped by your intellect.
So if we've attained something that is our knowledge in some deep way, but it's not grasped by our intellect, we can't really even talk about it, right?
This explains the big problem that we have whenever we leave one of these retreats.
We always have a big problem.
Sometimes people ask about this, and I never have a good answer, either.
This was an amazing retreat.
I learned so much.
I don't know how to talk about it.
My friend, my spouse, my dog, somebody's going to ask me when I get home, what am I going to say?
Maybe now we know what to say.
We figured it out.
We could write this down on a little card so you remember it: "I do not suppose that what I have attained became my knowledge and is grasped by my intellect."
I take care of that conversation.
But there is no question that people have powerful experiences, and they are important, I think.
But are they essential, and do they happen to everybody?
No, I don't think so.
I've had some interesting experiences and I've talked to a lot of people who have, but sometimes it really doesn't feel like, so it never feels like this inevitable outcome of practice to me.
Everything we experience, everything that happens, is conditioned by so many factors.
Even a glimpse of the so-called unconditioned is conditioned by many factors.
It seems like a lot of times when people have some kind of big experience in meditation, they've had, prior to that, a hell of a lot of stress.
Maybe not immediately before, but maybe decades and decades before.
Some people are wired in such a way that there's this dam that's waiting to burst.
Psychically, psychologically, spiritually.
And so when that dam bursts, it's a big deal.
Sometimes the flood that washes over you is a great relief.
Other times it just tumbles you around and bonks you on the head.
It's not always a great thing to have a big experience in meditation anyway.
It does seem to have as much to do with personality and conditioning and conditions as it does any sort of inevitable and important outcome of anything.
Probably many of those conditions that lead to some people having big meditation experiences at some times and other people not will always stay mysterious to us.
It's like in the Yogachara philosophy, the dark storehouse of universal consciousness.
You can't see what seeds are down there.
And for many of us, it's a more gradual thing.
We don't necessarily even notice while it's happening.
It's also something where you want to be a little bit careful what you wish for, anyhow.
I worked with one person for a while who had constant visions in meditation actually.
Full-blown visions where she would be somewhere else, in a waking state apparently, where she could see and hear a whole different world.
Often she would also simultaneously have some sense of being a body here sitting on the cushion.
But there would also be periods of time where that was not apparent to her.
Those would be sort of unknowable lengths of time.
Could have been half a second or half an hour till the bell rang.
And why did she come to ask me about all this?
She wanted to know, how can I make this stop?
I just get lost in these visions.
I don't think it's really helping me.
I agreed with her.
I didn't think it really was helping her.
So it's really hard to know.
Do visions and big experiences help us?
Is that enlightenment?
Is enlightenment quieter?
Is enlightenment knowable or unknowable?
Is anything we put in a word or a concept really the thing that we think it is?

Because maybe other times it's more like Dogen is saying, or maybe all the time, there may be something really important and transformational going on, but you might not know it in your thinking mind that wants stuff.
Your mind that is so conditioned by the story of me and what I think should be happening or shouldn't be happening here.
I was just sharing some stories about coming to Samish once a year.
For me this has always been this kind of surprising checkpoint.
I don't think about it till after I get here, but after I get here I say, wow, I'm back here.
And I think about all the things that have happened here over the years, in my life, in my practice.
Some challenging things have happened here and some wonderful things.
I can suddenly notice, oh my gosh, whoever this is that I call me is really changing over the years.
I feel very differently now in these ways that I'm coming back into view, because I'm looking at that person or that little plywood cabin there and remembering how things have been before.
Sometimes I notice just an absence of something when I come to sesshin.
Oh yeah, that's true.
I used to start sesshin really rattled, really wired, really busy mind.
Huh, not this time.
Where'd the busy mind go?
I'll probably be back, but he's not here at the moment.
Or, boy, that guy really used to trigger me.
But wait, no trigger.
What happened?
Has he changed?
Have I changed?
Is it just luck?
In those cases, I'm still a little on edge.
Like the trigger could still happen.
It just hasn't happened.
Maybe it won't happen.
Maybe it will.
There's a reason why we do this in groups.
Very supportive.
And as you probably know, there's a very old debate in Zen about sudden versus gradual approaches.
Is this progression to something called enlightenment, if there is such a thing, a sudden thing or a gradual thing?
I think probably saying sudden versus gradual, it's the "versus" that's most problematic.
Maybe it's both sudden and gradual, all mixed together.
And the other piece in these Zen stories is that when we read, hearing that so-and-so got enlightened, it's actually shorthand for a much bigger story, a much bigger process of practice.
It's really important to remember that when you read these stories, when part of your mind's like, huh, when's that going to happen to me?
Or more likely, darn, that will never happen to me.
What's implied here is this student has already practiced full-time for at least several years, maybe many, many years, in intense training environments under really strong teachers.
And so there's already been a lot going on.
A lot of things have happened.
A lot is turning and turning and being pressed on and moving and shifting inside.
And then, somehow, one more thing happens and there's some kind of obvious experience for the student, for the teacher, something we could write down in history books.
And of course, what gets written down in history books is often written much later, so we don't really know exactly what happened in a historical way.
But in any case, this final exchange with Yunmen was enough to shift something in Dongshan.
The tough night of yes and no thinking, the early morning encounter, this strong question: what are you doing?
Why are you always running off here and there to practice?
Which Dogen, you might have noticed, criticized a little bit just this morning.
Why are we always going off to the dusty realms?
Our seat is right here at home.
But nonetheless, these are powerful stories and they're important.
There are so many ways to hold them.
But one of the things I love about this story is the honoring of the awful night.
We also sometimes need tough nights, tough conditions when we're not too happy.
When I was at the monastery years ago, I remember I kind of bottomed out about the middle of the training period.
I was kind of coming back a little bit when I realized, oh, it's really when I'm at the end of my rope here that I'll really learn something.
I came to that reluctant realization.
I won't tell you my stories from that.
They're getting pretty old anyway.
Not as old as this story though.
And in our lineage family, we value accessibility, like I was saying.
And so we're not very good at this kind of tough Zen talk.
I don't really know how to do it.
And Norman doesn't really know how to do it either, so I couldn't really learn it from him.
This challenging way of talking, where you sense somehow that this student's kind of on the edge of something.
If I push a little bit, it would really be compassionate.
If I yell right now, ha!
There's a famous shout that the Rinzai teachers do, which is something like, Katz!
K-A-T-Z.
It's Romanized.
Katz!
That's way louder.
Way louder.
And it should be a complete surprise too.
But I have had the good fortune to encounter a few teachers who were more in that mode.
And I don't know if it's even always that deliberate.
Soon after Norman, [unclear: "back to the archetype of ordination"], since that's an important thing that we believe to be real.
Not so long after Norman asked me to ordain, I was going out to dinner, just minding my own business, with some Zen friends and a visiting teacher.
And that teacher turns to me in the lobby right before we walk to the table, looks me in the eye and says, so, I hear Norman's ordaining you.
How will you train?
And then, your table's ready.
I go in.
I spend the rest of the meal, and the rest of some months, in an ocean of yes and no thinking.
And I don't know if she was trying to challenge me, or if she didn't trust Norman's way of doing things, or if she was just curious.
Maybe she just wanted to know, was Norman going to come to Bellingham, or was I going to go to Tassajara, or did I need some help?
Maybe she was offering to help me.
But I received it as a tough teaching.
Who do you think you are?
With your once-a-week sitting group in some podunk town in the outskirts, taking on this great role of Zen priest.
It was hard, actually.
It was really hard to take.
But I learned something.
So I think it wouldn't be the worst for all of us at some point to have a tough Zen encounter.
Go to some place where they say, who are you?
Where do you come from?
I come from Bellingham.
Bellingham.
Now I'm on this national teacher email list, they've probably heard of me, unfortunately for you.
Oh, Tim.
But we don't really need these tough teachers, actually.
We're our own tough teacher, aren't we?
There's always some little guy or gal in our head asking these challenging questions anyway.
Who do you think you are?
Where do you come from?
What are you doing going off here and there to practice?
Luckily, and according to our school, luckily for us, we're already enlightened, so it's okay.
But we have to practice the rest of our life to express that and actualize that.
So that's my take on case 15, Dung Shun's encounter with Yun Men.
*Dung Shun came to study with Yun Men.
Yun Men asked, where are you from?
From Cha Du, Dung Shun replied.
Where were you during the summer?
Well, I was at Baoshui monastery in Hunan.
When did you leave there, Yun Men asked?
On August 25th, was Dung Shun's reply.
I spare you 60 blows, Yun Men said.
The next day Dung Shun came to Yun Men and said, yesterday you said you spared me 60 blows.
I don't know what my mistake is.
You rice bag, shouted Yun Men.
What makes you wander about now west of the river, now south of the lake?
And at this, Dung Shun got enlightenment.*
So, I've had a song stuck in my head, and since I have the bully pulpit, I'm going to trust that impulse and we can sing a song.
The song stuck in my head is Cat Stevens, "Father and Son."
I don't know why, but it's a very male song, I know, and we're mostly not male people here.
Maybe it came to my head because these stories are so very male and so very much involve the father and son archetype.
The young monk is the son seeking out a wise teacher, a wise father, and then it happens in this multi-generational way.
The son grows up in these stories.
There'll be a later koan in the book where the one who was the student is now the teacher, now the father teaching a new son.
And I told you one of my Norman father and son stories yesterday, maybe that's in there too.
I was so touched that he wanted to practice with me.
Didn't know that he was going to be my daddy.
Another time, okay, one monastery story.
I'm at the monastery for three months getting really tweaked out and exhausted.
I don't know if I knew this ahead or if it was decided later, but I'm not with my main teacher or anyone I really knew that much before getting there.
I'm making some friends, but I'm kind of bottomed out.
And then Norman's coming.
Yeah.
Norman's coming.
He's going to be there for like two weeks.
He's going to teach a class.
I get to tell him all my problems.
I'm so happy.
I'm so excited.
Like really excited.
Look, it's vibrating.
And my first encounter with Norman is in the coffee-tea area.
My great stories happen in lobbies and by the coffee pod, not in the zendo.
And he looks at me, says hi.
I don't know if there was a hug or not, and he says to me right away, I'm going to be pretty busy.
It's good to see you, but I might not be able to see you much.
Very helpful.
All right, so you're going to have to imagine the rhythm guitar and the little piano lick that happens in the transition between the father parts and the son parts.
There's not exactly a chorus, although the father part is repeated, so it's kind of a long chorus.
And you're welcome to sing if you know the song.
I'm sorry to insist on singing it, but it seems like I'm going to.

Just relax and take it easy.
You're still young.
That's your fault.
There's so much you have to know.
Find a girl.
Settle down.
If you want to, you can marry.
Look at me.
I am old, but I'm happy.
I was once like you are now, and I know that it's not easy to be calm when you found something going on.

*How can I try to explain?
When I do, he turns away again, and it's always been the same, same old story.
From the moment I could talk, I was ordered to listen.
Now there's a way, and I know that I have to go away.
I know I have to go.*
*It's not time to make a change.
Just sit down and take it slowly.
You're still young.
That's your fault.
There's so much you have to go through.
Find a girl.
Settle down.
If you want to, you can marry.

*All the times that I cried, keeping all the things I knew inside.
It's hard, but it's harder to ignore it.
If you were right, I'd agree.
But it's them you know, not me now.
Now there's a way, and I know that I have to go away.
I know I have to go.*
Piano.
*I know I have to go.*
I don't know.
Maybe we can map that as an internal struggle, too.
It's great.
You can psychologize anything if you want to.
What are the voices in us that want us to be stable and patient and look at the big picture?
What are the voices in us that are just like, damn it, I want something different.
I want to change.
I don't want to be like that.
I want to be somebody wiser, somebody better, somebody enlightened.
And maybe sudden and gradual, we need both voices.
Both voices.
So, thanks for listening so patiently.
Isn't it nice, I don't know if you really feel this way, but I will map this on you anyway.
Isn't it nice to settle in a little bit to this routine, so today we'll just do like yesterday, tomorrow we'll start out the same.
Just kind of get in the rhythm of this thing.
So simple.
Sitting, breathing, listening, eating, shoveling wood chips around, painting.
How could we really have any problems?
It's all worked out.
And so maybe there's a way that it's all worked out even when we're not in this particular circumstance.
Just relax and take it easy, as I said in there.
